title: Q2 2026 Earnings Release (8-K, filed 2026-07-31)
analysis:
- **Downstream earnings exploded to $4.9B** ($2.4B US + $2.5B international) vs $737M a year ago — the margin capture behind this summer's record crack spreads, on total earnings of $12.1B (21% ROCE, Brent averaging $104).
- **US refineries ran flat-out**: record crude unit throughput of 1.07 MMbpd at >97% utilization — yet US refined product sales fell 4% on weaker gasoline demand. This is a margin story, not a volume story.
- **The Middle East conflict is visibly cutting international product supply**: international refinery inputs down 10%, product sales down 13% on supply disruptions.
- **Retreating from Asian downstream**: sold Hong Kong fuels business; agreed to sell its 50% of Singapore Refining Company plus downstream assets across Vietnam, Australia, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Malaysia (closing 2027).
- Record $8.4B debt paydown in the quarter; $3B structural cost target hit six months early; Hess synergies at $1.5B run-rate.

**Signal for fuels markets**: a major running US refining at physical limits into record margins while shedding international downstream — more evidence that usable product supply, not crude, is the binding constraint.

title: Q2 2026 Earnings Release (8-K, filed 2026-07-31)
analysis:
- **Energy Products (refining) adjusted earnings hit $4.1B for the quarter** — first-half 2026 at $6.9B vs $2.2B in all of 1H 2025, a tripling driven by product margins.
- **Record second-quarter diesel production** (best in their data back to 2014) on strong US Gulf Coast utilization — the industry's max-distillate shift, quantified.
- Product placement flexed around the Middle East disruptions ($900M of YTD earnings impacts, plus an $884M non-US Energy Products impairment); energy products sales rose to 5.7 MMbpd.
- Total: $14.5B GAAP / $14.7B adjusted earnings, $17.2B free cash flow, $9.4B returned to shareholders in the quarter.
- **Corporate note**: completed its redomiciliation July 1 — ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation (Texas) replaced the New Jersey parent; same ticker, new SEC registrant.

**Signal for fuels markets**: the largest US refiner by complexity is running record diesel output into a supply-constrained market and still can't soften cracks — confirmation of how tight distillate supply actually is.

title: Q2 2026 Earnings Release (8-K, filed 2026-08-07)
analysis:
- **Fuel margin expansion all the way downstream**: gasoline distribution product margin jumped to $175.0M from $137.9M on higher cents-per-gallon margins — distributors are capturing spread, not just passing through higher prices.
- Adjusted EBITDA +51% to $148.2M; net income nearly tripled to $71.0M; distributable cash flow up 78% to $92.6M.
- Wholesale gasoline/blendstocks margin rose to $78.4M (from $58.8M) on favorable gasoline conditions; distillates/residual margin slipped to $28.1M; bunkering strengthened.
- Total sales of $6.8B vs $4.6B — almost entirely price-driven, mirroring the commodity move.
- Station operations margin flat (~$70M) — the c-store side is steady while the fuel side swings.

**Signal for fuels markets**: price volatility is profit for the distribution layer — Northeast rack-to-retail spreads are wide, and the margin expansion GLP shows suggests pump prices have room to keep rising even if wholesale stabilizes.

title: Q3 FY2026 Earnings Release (8-K, filed 2026-05-28)
analysis:
- **Gasoline was a major comp driver**: US comparable sales rose 9.4% reported but only 6.8% excluding gas prices and FX — fuel-price inflation contributed roughly 2.6 points, one of the largest gas contributions to comps in years (quarter ended May 10, before the summer spike accelerated).
- Fiscal Q3 (12 weeks): net sales $69.2B (+11.6%), net income $2.19B ($4.93/share); 931 warehouses, 639 in the US.
- The release gives no gallon or fuel-margin detail (Costco reserves that for the earnings call) — but the reported-vs-adjusted comp gap is the cleanest public marker of member fuel spending.
- Membership fees +10.7% to $1.37B — the model that lets Costco run fuel at thin margins as a traffic driver is compounding.

**Signal for fuels markets**: high-volume discount retail is passing higher fuel prices straight into reported sales while using cheap gas as a membership draw — expect Costco to stay the price floor in its markets. Fiscal Q4 (report due late September) will capture the full summer price surge.

title: Investor Presentation — April 2026
analysis:
- **Benicia is out**: buried in a slide-34 footnote — the Benicia refinery's processing units were idled in April 2026, leaving Wilmington (85 kbpd crude) as Valero's only California refinery. Portfolio now stands at 14 refineries, 3.0 MMbpd throughput / 2.5 MMbpd crude capacity, 61% concentrated on the Gulf Coast.
- **SAF is live at scale**: DGD Port Arthur SAF project (completed 4Q24) can upgrade up to 235M gal/yr — half the plant's renewable diesel output — to SAF for $315M total cost, expected to clear the 25% after-tax IRR hurdle. Total DGD platform: 1.22B gal/yr.
- **Renewable diesel is self-funded and best-in-class**: DGD cumulative EBITDA of $3,005M (VLO share) now exceeds cumulative capex of $2,071M. 2025 adjusted EBITDA of $0.59/gal led all RD peers ($0.21 peer average; some peers negative) — though well below the $2+/gal LCFS-era peaks of 2021–22.
- **Refining discipline over growth**: no new capacity — capital goes to optimization (St. Charles FCC project, $230M, 2H26 completion, +15 kbpd resid processing and +6 kbpd alkylate) at a 25% IRR hurdle. Lowest cash opex/bbl vs PSX/MPC/DINO/PBF; 2025 was their best-ever year for safety and mechanical availability.
- **Cash returned, not reinvested in barrels**: $4.0B returned in 2025 (67% payout), share count down 46% since 2012, dividend at $4.80 annualized for 2026, ~$1.4B sustaining capex.
- **Export lean**: >1.5 MMbpd ratable wholesale supply (>50% of light products), 349 kbpd exports in 2025, with Latin America taking 75% of US product exports as regional refining runs decline.

**Signal for fuels markets**: America's largest independent refiner is shrinking West Coast supply, capping domestic capacity growth in favor of buybacks, and steering its renewables platform toward mandated SAF markets — a structurally tightening posture for US refined product supply, especially California gasoline and diesel/jet.
